Vide this appeal, the appellant has challenged the order dated 06.09.2018 of Ld. Adjudicating Officer/Additional District Magistrate (New Delhi), Delhi ("ADM" in short) directing the appellants no. 1 & 2 (partner of the supplier firm and the firm) to pay a consolidated penalty of Rs.30,000/
and appellants no.3 & 4 (director & nominee, respectively of manufacturing company) to pay a consolidated penalty of Rs.60,000/ under Section 52 of the Food Safety and Standard Act, 2006 ("FSS Act" in short) for violation of Sections 26(2)(ii), 23(1) & 27(3)(c) read with Section 3(1)(zf)(c)(i) of FSS Act and Regulation 2.2.2.2(f)(i) of The Food Safety and Standards(Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011 ("FSS(P&L) Regulations" in short) for selling misbranded food.

3.0 The appellant has challenged the impugned order on the following grounds:
(i) the Ld. ADM failed to appreciate that the mixed fruit jam is a standardized product and was not being sold as mixture or combination of foods; label of standardized products are not required to declare the percentage of ingredients.

Hence , Regulation 2.2.2.2(f) Mr.Sandeep Sudhan & Ors. vs State, FSO Page No.4 of 15 :: 5 ::

The only requirement for the standardized food article/ mixed fruit jam is to give the names or ingredients as per 2.2.2.2(b) of FSS(P&L) Regulations;
(ii) Section 32 FSS Act mandates that prosecution should not be initiated for minor defects like the labelling defect in the instant case.

sentences.text: In view of the same, imposition of penalty on the director and nominee of the said company i.e. appellants no.3&4 is illegal.

Reliance in this respect is placed upon the judgment of Delhi High Court in MCD vs Kishan Chand and another dated 25.03.1975 in Criminal Appeal No.122/72.

sentences.text: On the other hand, Ld.Chief Public Prosecutor for the State sought dismissal of this appeal with heavy cost.

It was submitted that during the proceedings before the Ld.ADM, the appellants themselves pleaded that they have now corrected the deficiency in the label and even placed on record, the subsequent package/label after correction.
Same shows admission on their part of non compliance of Regulation 2.2.2.2(f)(i) of FSS(P&L) Regulations.
The said violation amounted to mis branding in terms of Section 3(1)(zf)(c)(i) FSS Act.
Section 52 FSS Act prescribes a penalty of upto Rs.Three Lacs for sale etc. of misbranded food.

But, the Ld.ADM imposed a consolidated penalty of only Rs.30,000/ on appellants no. 1 & 2 and a consolidated penalty of only Rs.60,000/ on appellants no.3 & 4.
5.0
I have heard Ld. Counsel for the appellant and Ld.Chief Public Prosecutor for the State and have perused the record carefully.

6.0 Let me at the outset refer to Regulation 2.2.2.2(f)(i) FSS(P&L) Regulations:
"2.2.2: Labelling of Prepackaged Foods

4 (f) Every package of food sold as a mixture or combination shall disclose the percentage of the ingredient used at the time of the manufacture of the food (including compound ingredients or categories of ingredients),if such ingredient- (i) is emphasised as present on the label through words or pictures or graphics; or"
6.1

From the above it is evident that any food article which is a combination/mixture and sold in a packaged form shall disclose on the package, the percentage of each of the ingredients used at the time of manufacturing of the said food, if such ingredient is emphasised as present on the label through words or pictures or Mr.Sandeep Sudhan & Ors. vs State, FSO Page No.8 of 15 :: 9 ::

sentences.text: Sample food article is Mixed Fruit Jam which admittedly consisted of different fruits and other ingredients.
Further, from the package of the sample food article on record, it is seen that pictures of various fruits viz. Cherry, Pineapple, Peer,
Grapes
etc . appear on the package
. In view of the same, the package of the sample food article/Mixed Fruit Jam undoubtedly required to comply with the above Regulation and mention the percentage of the ingredients used.
6.2 Admittedly, the package did not mention the percentage of the ingredients used.
As per the appellants themselves, the same was subsequently corrected and the same was even filed before the Ld.ADM.
6.3 In view of the above facts & circumstances, there is hardly any force in the appellant's contention that the aforesaid Regulation 2.2.2.2(f)(i) did not apply to the sample food article.
7.0 It would be pertinent to mention here that Section 23(1) FSS Act requires that no one shall manufacture, distribute, sell any packaged food products which is not labelled as per regulations.

Section 23(1) reads as under: "23. Packaging and labelling of foods.(1) No person shall manufacture, distribute, sell or expose for sale or despatch or deliver to any agent or broker for the Mr.Sandeep Sudhan & Ors. vs State, FSO Page No.9 of 15 :: 10 ::
purpose of sale, any packaged food products which are not marked and labelled in the manner as may be specified by regulations:

7.1 Further,such noncompliance renders a packaged food article misbranded in terms of Section 3(1)(zf)(c)(i) of FSS Act.

In view of the above provisions of law, the supplier / appellants no.1&2 as well as the representative of the manufacturer/ appellants no.3&4 are liable for manufacturing/sale/supply of misbranded sample food article.

8.0 The appellants no.1&2 have contended that they had sold / supplied the sample food article to M/s The Leela Palace in the same sealed condition in which it was purchased from the manufacturer company M/s Vidya Sagar Food Pvt. Ltd.vide valid invoices.
Thus, they were entitled for benefit u/S 80(B)(2)(a)(d)(e) FSS Act.).
8.1 Let me refer here to Section 80(B)(2) of FSS Act, under which the benefit of defence is sought.

Same reads as under :
"80. Defences which may or may not be allowed in prosecution under this Act.
(A)...

(B) Defence of due diligence  (1)...

sentences.text: From the plain reading of Section 80 (B)(2), it is evident that for claiming benefit under the said provision, besides selling the food in the same condition in which it was purchased it has to be proved by the person that he/it carried out checks of the food concerned, as were reasonable in all the circumstances.
8.2 The appellants no.1&2 have failed to demonstrate that they had carried out reasonable checks of the sample food article.

The Mr.Sandeep Sudhan & Ors. vs State, FSO Page No.12 of 15 :: 13 ::
appellants did not check that the label/package of the sample food article did not mention the percentage of ingredients as required under 2.2.2.2(f)(i) FSS(P&L)

sentences.text: 8.3.1 It is seen that the Ld.ADM found the manufacturer as well as supplier guilty of the aforesaid violations.
But while awarding penalty, the Ld.ADM has imposed a consolidated penalty of Rs.60,000/ on the appellants no. 3 & 4 i.e. director and nominee of manufacturing company.
No penalty has been imposed on the manufacturing company.

9.0 Another error which is noted in the impugned order, is that while concluding the violations,
Ld.ADM has recorded the violations as 26(2)(ii), 23(1) & 27(3)(c) read with Section 3(1)(zf)(c)
(i) of FSS Act and Regulation 2.2.2.3 and 2.2.2.10 of FSS(P&L) Regulations.

Whereas, the appellants have been found guilty of Mr.Sandeep Sudhan & Ors. vs State, FSO Page No.13 of 15 :: 14 ::
violation of regulation 2.2.2.2(f)(i) of the said Regulation and not Regulation 2.2.2.3 and 2.2.2.10.
9.1

In view of the above facts and circumstances, the matter needs to be remanded back to Ld. ADM for recording specific findings w.r.t. liability of the manufacturing company and also for necessary correction w.r.t. regulation, for violation of which,
the appellants have been penalised.

10.0 The appellants have also contended that Delhi Food Laboratory in which the sample was analyzed and issued analytical report, is not legally competent lab to analyze the samples of food under FSS Act as per Section 43 of FSS Act; as the same is neither NABL Accredited nor notified in the Official Gazette as per provisions Section 3(1)(p) FSS Act.
It is also contended that no penalty should have been imposed on the appellants as Section 32 FSS Act mandates that prosecution should not be initiated for minor defects.
10.1 It is seen that no such pleas were raised before the Ld.ADM earlier.
Be that as it may.
Let the Ld. ADM also consider the same.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In view of the above provisions of law, the supplier / appellants no.1&2 as well as the representative of the manufacturer/ appellants no.3&4 are liable for manufacturing/sale/supply of misbranded sample food article.
Thus, they were entitled for benefit u/S 80(B)(2)(a)(d)(e) FSS Act.).
From the plain reading of Section 80 (B)(2), it is evident that for claiming benefit under the said provision, besides selling the food in the same condition in which it was purchased it has to be proved by the person that he/it carried out checks of the food concerned, as were reasonable in all the circumstances.
8.2 The appellants no.1&2 have failed to demonstrate that they had carried out reasonable checks of the sample food article.
Thus they failed to exercise due diligence before selling the food article.
In view of these facts and circumstances, the appellants have failed to demonstrate that they are entitled to the benefit of Section 80 (B)(2) FSS Act.
8.3
10.0 The appellants have also contended that Delhi Food Laboratory in which the sample was analyzed and issued analytical report, is not legally competent lab to analyze the samples of food under FSS Act as per Section 43 of FSS Act; as the same is neither NABL Accredited nor notified in the Official Gazette as per provisions Section 3(1)(p) FSS Act.
